evidence.claim: The paper overstates its main theoretical claim by asserting ExTernD 'provably reaches any target accuracy' at practical settings, when the proved geometric bound only holds in the limit with much larger k than used in experiments.
evidence.excerpt: the paper's headline theoretical claim is that ExTernD "provably reaches any target accuracy" and "approaches bf16 accuracy arbitrarily closely". This is technically true, but Prop. 2's geometric rate is $(1-1/mn)^k$, so pushing the residual below any nontrivial $\varepsilon$ needs $k = \Theta(mn\log\|A\|/\varepsilon)$ — many orders of magnitude beyond the $k\sim 2.5\text{–}3\min(m,n)$ regime the paper actually uses ($k/mn$ of order $10^{-3}$–$10^{-4}$ for typical LLM matrices). The theoretical result therefore cannot support the practical framing that "any accuracy target is hit exactly"...

judge_panel.reason: The paper does acknowledge in Appendix A that the geometric bound is loose ('empirical convergence is much faster than geometric in mn (99% energy at µ ≈ 2.5–3)'), but the headline claim that ExTernD 'provably reaches any target accuracy' rests on Prop. 2's single-entry safeguard, which theoretically requires k = Θ(mn log‖A‖/ε) steps—far beyond practical µ values. The paper does not quantify how the practical regime relates to the theoretical guarantee, leaving the strong framing partially unsupported, though the paper is transparent that the safeguard 'never activates in practice.'

The paper uses strong practical-sounding language — e.g. the Abstract says the error "can be driven below any ε > 0" and the Introduction says "a target accuracy be hit exactly rather than rounded up to the next bit-width" — but Appendix A only proves the asymptotic existence claim: "For every ε > 0 there is a finite inner rank k with ∥A − B diag(D)C∥F < ε." It does not quantify what k is needed in the practical µ≈2–3 regime used in experiments.

The reviewer incorrectly conflates two separate claims. The paper does not use the theoretical bound to claim that an accuracy target is hit "exactly"; rather, it attributes this exactness to the continuity of its parameters: "multiplier µ ... and a sparsity threshold τ ... can each be set per matrix to any real value, letting a target accuracy be hit exactly rather than rounded up." Furthermore, the paper explicitly acknowledges the gap between the theoretical bound and practical settings in Appendix A: "empirical convergence is much faster than geometric in mn (99% energy at µ ≈ 2.5–3)."
